generatedProse.concept-context: Study material comes in very different shapes, and the three families of technique fit different shapes. A set of linked ideas, where parts connect into a whole, suits a visual map that shows how the pieces fit together. A set of terms or definitions suits flashcards or reading aloud. A procedure or sequence of steps suits a physical walk-through. Choosing well means looking at the material first, rather than reaching for the same method every time.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students revising the same module, which has three very different topics: a set of linked ideas, a list of key terms, and the steps of a set procedure.

Student A likes flashcards, so he makes flashcards for all three. The terms suit cards well. But the set of linked ideas becomes a pile of cards in no order, and the connections between the parts are lost. The procedure, which only makes sense as a sequence, does not fit cards at all. The technique was fine; using the same one for everything was not.

Student B looks at each topic first. The key terms become flashcards. The linked ideas become a visual map that lays out the parts and shows how they connect. The procedure becomes a physical walk-through, stepping through each stage in order. Each technique was chosen to fit what the topic is.

Both students revised all three topics. Only Student B matched the technique to the material rather than forcing one method onto everything.
generatedProse.summary: Active techniques fall into three families: visual, auditory and kinaesthetic. A set of linked ideas suits a visual map, a set of terms suits flashcards or reading aloud, and a procedure suits a kinaesthetic walk-through. None is better than the others; the skill is matching the technique to the material. You can now describe the families, place a technique in its family, and choose techniques that fit what you are revising.

check.body: In the worked example, why did Student B use a visual map for the linked ideas and flashcards for the key terms?

items.text: She matched each technique to the kind of material, rather than using one method for everything.
She preferred variety and wanted her revision to feel less boring.
She had run out of flashcards and had to improvise.
Visual maps are always better than flashcards.

feedback.correct: That's right. Student B chose each technique to fit the kind of material, which is selecting to fit.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the reason that is about matching the method to the material.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B matched each technique to the kind of material, rather than forcing one method onto everything. It was not about variety, chance or one technique being best.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
